title: Brill Pays
passages:
Rhea cut the flatbed's engine forty meters short of Marrow Cut's door plate. The exhaust ticked as it cooled. She climbed down with Teodoro's written order folded in her hand and walked to the concrete pad where Dray stood planted, hands in his coat.

"Reader two logged eleven canisters at Culvert Nine's jaw as Anza salvage," Rhea said, holding out the paper. "That's an order, not a request. My node is sending a flatbed to haul them back."

Dray didn't take it. He looked at the shed behind him, then at her flatbed. "A blank rig is a parts pile," he said. "A rig lives while a living name is wired to its crew plate. The cans in that jaw have no plate. No name. No one to answer for them."

"They have a log," Rhea said. "And my brother is breathing on Anza mains compressor power because of those cans. I don't trade names. I haul cargo."

Dray shifted his weight. "I mean to buy them with a name. One name, wired to plate 4217 — Rig Seven, dark eleven months — before two witnesses. Without it, nothing in this shed moves. Not the cans, not my rigs, not you."

Rhea looked past him at the shed door. She could see the dim glow of Amil's bench inside. She had trusted a truck's diagnostics more than a person's word her whole life. She trusted the reader's log more than Dray's book.

"Then you'll wait a long time," she said. "My flatbed's got fuel and no schedule."

She turned and walked back to the cab. The door plate rattled as she swung up into the seat. She dropped the order onto the dash and started the engine. The transmission whined into gear.

Dray shouted after her, "The reader's log doesn't feed a crew through winter!"

"It feeds my brother," Rhea said, and released the brake.

The flatbed lurched forward, tires spitting gravel. She aimed for the spur, the narrow track that ran back down to Culvert Nine's jaw. If she beat Dray there, she could slap Teodoro's order on the receiving plate and have Brill crank the jaw open before Dray could wire a name to anything.

In her side mirror, Rig Seven's headlight stayed dark inside the shed. Behind her, Dray's rig coughed to life, its own lamps sweeping across the yard. Her transponder blinked red on the dash. Teodoro's order wasn't worth the paper it was printed on if Dray was coming down the spur after her.
